h: The pen in Emergency 2.0: why journalists are standing alone
dek: According to Pamela Philipose, today's repression is darker partly because journalists are not standing with one another.
body: In her column Backstory in The Wire, Pamela Philipose raises an uncomfortable question: which was the worse time for journalists, Indira Gandhi's twenty-one-month Emergency or today, which she calls an undeclared Emergency 2.0.

First she recalls the courage Indian journalism showed after the Emergency. There was reporting on the blinding of 31 prisoners in Bhagalpur jail, a sting on the buying and selling of women in Dholpur, and in Bhopal Rajkumar Keswani warned of the danger from the Union Carbide factory.

According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, Delhi Police detained 43 media workers during the protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Journalists were shoved, their equipment snatched, and they were asked for press cards to report on an open street. At least three women journalists complained of sexual harassment. On 3 October at Jantar Mantar, independent journalist Rosy accused ACP Vivek Bhagat of misconduct; in response the officer complained that she had made a casteist remark, and now the FIR is against the journalist herself. Indira Jaising went to the Supreme Court, where Chief Justice Surya Kant sought an answer from a senior Delhi Police officer.

The writer is also angry with the Press Council of India. According to her, instead of condemning the attacks, the Council advised those covering the protests to stay neutral and carry first-aid kits. On 16 October journalists gathered at the Press Club of India to think about how to protect themselves.

But the article's real blow is about solidarity. Philipose recalls that during the Emergency, Kuldip Nayar called a meeting of Delhi's journalists on 29 June 1975 and was himself arrested a month later. According to her, a privileged section of today's media seems indifferent to how its own colleagues are being treated, and this difference makes the present moment more dangerous.
nazar: This movement stands on one question: whose names were cut from the voter list, and why. In such a moment, picking a reporter up off the street is putting a lock on information itself. What is never seen can never be held to account.
Philipose's complaint is with the big channels and their faces, but the question is for every newsroom. On the day a woman journalist is hit with a counter-case, silence too is choosing a side.
sawal: When fellow journalists are picked up, why is the rest of the media silent?
ref: Kuldip Nayar
A well-known journalist and writer who openly opposed censorship during the 1975 Emergency and went to jail. He later served as India's High Commissioner to Britain and as a Rajya Sabha member.
Press Council of India
A statutory body set up to protect press freedom and set standards for journalism. Its present form comes from a 1978 law.
ank: Media workers detained, according to CPJ
Women journalists who complained of sexual harassment (at least)

h: Democracy in reverse: the government is choosing the people, not the other way round
dek: Arun Kumar Tripathi argues that after 13 crore names were cut, the noise about 'regime change' is an attempt to divert attention from the real question.
body: Senior journalist Arun Kumar Tripathi writes in Samata Marg that Indian democracy is turning into a spectacle. Democracy means citizens choose their rulers and change them if needed. Here the opposite is happening: the government is choosing its voters and pushing people settled for years off the list. He recalls Bertolt Brecht's 1953 poem that mocks a government which dissolves the people and elects a new one.

According to the writer, the SIR that began in Bihar on 25 June 2025 has now spread across the country and more than 13 crore people have been left off the list. The effect of a name being cut does not stop at the vote; it reaches rations, healthcare, education, jobs, scholarships and passports.

The most serious issue is transparency. Right to Information activist Anjali Bhardwaj asked who took the decision for a nationwide SIR. According to the writer, the Commission replied that the decision was not its own and that it had no information. When a copy was sought of what had been called an 'independent review' in court, the Commission said it had no such paper either.

When people demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, the answer came as repression: a ban at Jantar Mantar, restrictions even on hoisting the tricolour, and then the bogey of 'regime change'. The writer reminds us that this term is usually used for a coup, a rebellion or foreign interference. Changing voters' minds and changing the government through elections is the everyday process of democracy; calling it a conspiracy is a game of words.

His conclusion is that the country is caught between two things: a movement that wants to change the government, and a government that is changing the voters to stay in power. This dispute should have been settled in court. It was not, so it came out onto the street.
nazar: Tripathi's sharpest question is who finally took the decision to remove 13 crore people from the list, when the Commission itself says it does not know. A process that has no owner is one for which no one will take responsibility either.
The 'regime change' debate is really a way to avoid the voter list debate. Wanting to change the government is no crime in a democracy. Changing the voters certainly is.
sawal: Who decided to cut 13 crore names?
ref: Bertolt Brecht
German poet and playwright. His satirical poem 'The Solution', written after the 1953 workers' uprising in East Germany, is a famous comment on the arrogance of power.
SIR (Special Intensive Revision)
A door-to-door check of the voter list in which voters were asked for documents. It is alleged that the names of crores of eligible citizens were cut in it.

h: Old script, new public: why the smear campaign is not working
dek: Sagarika Ghose argues that charges of a 'foreign hand', 'urban Naxals' and 'regime change' are worn out, while the government has no answer to the figures on deleted names.
body: This article by Sagarika Ghose, Trinamool Congress Rajya Sabha MP and journalist, appeared in ThePrint Hindi, and there is an English version too. She writes that the young people of the Cockroach Janata Party have returned to the barricades even after some of their leaders were arrested, and the opposition too is not ready to back down. The demand is clear: Gyanesh Kumar's exit and a new Election Commission.

According to the writer, the government is opening the same old book: questioning the protesters' motives and hinting at some hidden hand behind them. But these charges no longer work. If SIR was meant to remove infiltrators, the government should say how many of the 13.39 crore names cut in three phases turned out to be foreigners. The writer says there has been no answer to RTI requests or questions in Parliament either. In Bengal, 93 percent of names were restored in the appeals that were heard, yet lakhs of appeals are still pending.

On the charge of 'foreign funding' she asks for proof and recalls that in the seventies Indira Gandhi played the same card. On the charge of 'anarchy' her question is who is spreading the disorder: the peaceful protesters, or the officials who shut the metro, removed Jantar Mantar from the list of protest sites and pushed people onto the roads.

The 'urban Naxal' label does not stick to this crowd either, which has students, professors, actors, doctors, parents and people on the street for the first time. On 'regime change' she says every opposition party wants to change the government through elections; calling this dangerous is a trick to stir anger on social media.

Her conclusion is that until the government says how many names were cut and why, how many foreigners were found, and what protection there is for names wrongly cut, every attempt to smear the movement will keep failing.
nazar: It should be remembered that the writer is herself an MP of an opposition party. But her questions belong to no party; they belong to every voter. If crores of names are cut in the name of infiltration and the count of infiltrators never comes out, suspicion is natural.
Names being restored in 93 percent of appeals in Bengal shows that the mistake was not the exception but the pattern. For those whose appeals have not yet been heard, what does their vote rest on?
sawal: Of the names cut in the name of infiltration, how many were infiltrators?
ref: 'Foreign hand'
A common charge of the Indira Gandhi government in the seventies, which blamed protests and movements on a conspiracy by foreign powers.
Urban Naxal
A term coined by government supporters, used to paint writers, lawyers and activists in cities as sympathisers of Maoists.

h: Neha Bora and the Left's new language: from reels to the street
dek: Outlook's cover story asks whether, through the AISA leader, Left politics is finding ground among a new generation.
body: In Outlook's cover story, Mrinalini Dhyani and Ashlin Mathew use AISA national president Neha Bora to ask whether the Indian Left is finding space among a new generation. The article opens with a scene from 4 October: a protester being dragged away from a barricade, smiling and flashing the victory sign.

Bora, 29, has about 12 lakh followers on Instagram, and her video criticising Yogi Adityanath in Gorakhpur on 14 September was viewed more than 70 lakh times. Raised in Khatima by a soldier father in a BJP-supporting family, Bora did street theatre at Aurobindo College, joined AISA in 2017 and became national president in 2023.

The writers see her as the next link after Kanhaiya Kumar in Delhi's Left student tradition, but her way of speaking belongs to the age of short videos. Their assessment is that for the first time since 2014, the ruling side's grip on young people's political debate looks loose. According to French political scientist Jean-Thomas Martelli, social media brings the crowds, while experienced activists like Bora take the first risk and teach newcomers to protest calmly.

BJP spokesperson Tuhin Sinha calls her Rahul Gandhi's pawn and links her to Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam. The article reminds us that branding Left student leaders as anti-national is an old weapon, and it also works in elections: Kanhaiya lost from Begusarai in 2019 by more than 4.2 lakh votes. Bora rejects speculation that she will join the Congress and says her future is with the CPI(ML).

A movement's popularity does not turn into votes on its own, though according to Martelli Indian democracy is becoming more protest-centred and the Left is stronger than it looks. By the article's reckoning, that victory sign is not yet success but a declaration of stubbornness.
nazar: Squeezing a movement into one face is an old media habit, and a risky one. Bora's strength comes from the organisation behind her and thousands of nameless young people, not from her follower count.
The anti-national label is being rolled out again. The question is whether, this time, the fear of names being cut from the voter list will prove bigger than that label.
sawal: How far will this movement go without a face?
ref: AISA
All India Students' Association, a Left student organisation linked to the CPI(ML) Liberation, with a strong presence in JNU and Delhi University.

h: From exams to the vote: the Cockroach movement's next test
dek: According to historian Adhip Amin, the CJP has broken Modi's dominance, but bigger change will come only from a bond between students and workers.
body: Adhip Amin, a history researcher at Princeton University, reads the movements in India and France side by side in his newsletter Dispatches From Another World. In the section on India, he traces the Cockroach Janata Party's journey from the start and sets out its limits along with its strength.

On 3 May 2026 about 23 lakh students sat the medical entrance exam, which was cancelled after a paper leak. In this period there were reports of 21 student suicides. A Chief Justice's remark calling unemployed young people cockroaches gave the movement its name, and the demand rose for Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. Lathis, tear gas and pellets were used; according to the article, Amnesty on 24 July identified a constable in Siwan firing an AK-type rifle. Pradhan resigned the very next day.

Amin explains that the CJP refused to become a party and chose the role of a public watchdog. In August Abhijeet Dipke defended reservations, and the Fix Our Schools campaign reached the shortage of teachers and unsafe buildings in government schools. The demands spread from the exam to the conditions of preparation and then to the structure of education.

In October the same movement is firm on the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Citing an Indian Express investigation, the writer notes that the other two commissioners had raised written objections at least fourteen times in ten months: over changes to registration rules, arbitrary deletion of names and centralised control of the voter database. The response was police violence and mass arrests.

Along with the praise, Amin sets a hard condition. Students entering politics on their own strength matters, but it is not enough for social change. The real test is whether the movement can manage the relationships within it, such as that between students and workers, and turn the separate groups that have come out into one shared force.
nazar: Among those whose names were cut in the SIR, a large number are said to be migrant workers and people from poor settlements. If the movement reaches those settlements as well as Jantar Mantar, the fight for the vote will join the fight for bread.
Amin's warning applies to opposition parties too: winning an election on borrowed youthful energy is easy, turning it into a lasting organisation is hard.
sawal: Will the student movement reach the workers' settlements?
ref: The Indian Express investigation
A report published on 23 September 2026 detailing the objections of the other two commissioners within the Election Commission. The demand for resignation grew sharper after it.
Cockroach Janata Party
An online platform set up as satire in summer 2026 in response to a Chief Justice's remark, which became a student movement against paper leaks.

h: From the right to vote to the right to protest: the Constitution is changing without amendment
dek: Sunil Kumar says that rights which exist on paper are being taken away every day on Delhi's streets, and this has not even needed a change to the Constitution.
body: In Janchowk's Beech Bahas column, Sunil Kumar recalls that from the first general election in 1952 every adult got the right to vote, and this right made the ordinary person feel that the government was one they had chosen. According to the writer, SIR is cutting into this right, and since 2 October citizens and opposition parties have been on Delhi's streets against it.

Gandhi Jayanti was chosen deliberately, in memory of satyagraha (Gandhi's non-violent resistance). The answer came as barricades, prohibitory orders, lathis and tear gas. According to the writer, 11 metro stations were shut, local trains were deliberately stopped, and those who reached were detained. He asks what became of the right to peaceful assembly under Article 19(1)(b).

A large part of the article is about the women journalists who on 3 October accused Delhi Police officers of sexual harassment. According to the writer, hundreds of independent journalists surrounded the police station to get an FIR, but the investigation was handed to the Crime Branch and the complainants themselves were picked up instead. A promotion was even announced for the accused officer, which was held back after criticism.

Drawing on old Supreme Court judgments and government data on custodial rape, the writer says police protecting their own is nothing new. Asking freelance journalists for identity cards and questioning them about their education is not the police's job; its job is to keep order.

His conclusion is that the rights to speak, to assemble and to vote are being hollowed out without any amendment. The talk in 2024 of 400 seats to change the Constitution now seems unnecessary. Like Ambedkar and Lohia, he says rights are not begged for, they are won by fighting.
nazar: The article's most important point is the link: the right to vote and the right to protest are not separate. Someone whose name was cut will come to the street with a complaint, and if the street is closed too, no door is left for them in a democracy.
The women journalists' charges are still charges, but only a fair investigation will show whether the police were managing the protest or crushing it.
sawal: If the street is closed too, where does a citizen take a complaint?
ref: Article 19(1)(b)
The provision of the Constitution that gives citizens the right to assemble peacefully and without arms, subject to reasonable restrictions.
Article 326
The article that gives every adult citizen the right to vote, on which universal adult franchise rests.

h: Bhagwat's Dussehra speech: an ideological shield that calls the movement a 'foreign storm'
dek: Anilesh S. Mahajan's analysis shows how the RSS chief tied the 'regime change' debate to the BJP's line, and the tests this has raised for the RSS.
body: In India Today Hindi, Anilesh S. Mahajan writes that in his Vijayadashami speech on 20 October, Mohan Bhagwat spoke of a 'storm' coming from the West that wants to overturn every order. Bangladesh, Nepal, France and Albania were listed as examples. No one was named, but Delhi took the line about 'ambitious leaders' as aimed at Rahul Gandhi. He also listed the limits of protest: it should have a purpose, stay within the Constitution and not chase cheap popularity.

According to the writer, five days before the speech Prashant Bhushan had spoken of 'regime change' at an anti-SIR press conference, and then Pawan Khera and AISA's Neha Bora repeated the same term. Bhagwat's speech gave ideological backing to the BJP's line that the movement is a 'toolkit' run from outside.

The article reminds us that the RSS has been demanding since 2012 that infiltrators be removed from voter lists, so SIR puts that very demand into practice. In Bengal about 90 lakh names were cut before the April election, nearly 12 percent of voters. Nagpur sees the victories in Bengal and Bihar as a success of this method; the opposition sees it as a threat to the credibility of the voter list.

The writer describes the Cockroach Janata Party as a loose movement born of satire, with about 1.9 crore followers on Instagram against the BJP's roughly 90 lakh. In other words, this movement is echoing louder among the very young people the RSS claims to reach.

According to Mahajan, the RSS faces three tests in its second century: whether diversity will be accepted only on Hindu terms, whether the standard of legitimate protest Bhagwat described will also apply to anti-government movements, and an accounting of its work. The answers will come from the Supreme Court, the street and the 2027 Uttar Pradesh election.
nazar: This analysis shows that the noise about 'regime change' is no longer just a TV debate but has ideological approval from the RSS platform. When cleaning up the voter list is itself an organisation's old demand, the questions about the Commission's fairness grow deeper.

The conditions for protest that Bhagwat listed are ones the movement meets: within the Constitution, peaceful, with a clear purpose. The real test is whether those in power accept these standards themselves.
sawal: Whom does calling peaceful protest a 'foreign storm' protect?
ref: Vijayadashami speech
The RSS chief's annual speech in Nagpur every Dussehra, seen as a signal of the ideological direction of the Sangh Parivar.
Regime change
An attempt to change a government, often in the sense of a coup or foreign interference. The opposition says it means changing power through elections.

h: Hindutva is not Hinduism: a political ideology hiding behind religion
dek: Deep Sharma argues that Hinduism and Hindutva have been deliberately merged so that every criticism of power can be called an attack on religion.
body: In his newsletter 'Fascism in India', Deep Sharma begins with a familiar question asked at home: what is wrong with a government that supports your own religion? According to him, this article is not an attack on Hinduism but a defence of it.

He argues that over the past twelve years the difference between Hinduism and Hindutva has been deliberately erased. Critics are first suppressed with cases and raids, and criticism that cannot be suppressed is called anti-Hindu or anti-national. As examples he lists the arrest of NewsClick journalists, the BJP's reaction after the Hindenburg report on Adani, and the attacks on Rahul Gandhi over his remark on the Manusmriti in August 2026.

The writer reminds us that Hinduism has no single founder, no single scripture and no central authority. Bhakti poets like Kabir, Mirabai and Tukaram are part of this tradition too, and they challenged caste from within. According to him, this very openness became a weakness before a new idea that arrived in 1923.

That idea was Vinayak Damodar Savarkar's book 'Hindutva', which he wrote while confined in Ratnagiri. According to the writer, Savarkar was himself an atheist and made fatherland, holy land and a shared race the conditions for being Hindu, which left Muslims and Christians out. Citing speeches from 1938 and research by historian Marzia Casolari, the writer says Savarkar praised Nazi Germany, and he links this thinking to Europe's racial nationalism.

In the end the writer likens Hindutva to the wooden horse of Troy: on the outside a cover of saffron, Ram and Sanskrit words, inside a demand for uniformity, a permanent enemy and an identity built on race. He says a religion thousands of years old survived without this hundred-year-old ideology.
nazar: The point about the difference between Hindutva and Hinduism is not new; Savarkar himself accepted that difference. The article's real question is where room for debate is left when criticism of a leader or a businessman starts being called an attack on faith. Historians differ on the relationship between Savarkar and fascism, and this article is the argument of one side, not a final verdict.

Still, in a country with the tradition of Kabir and Raidas, it is important to remember that the reach of faith is far bigger than any one party or organisation, and that the claim to save religion often shrinks its most open parts.
sawal: Who will decide the difference between faith and politics?
ref: Hindutva (1923)

Vinayak Damodar Savarkar's book, whose full title is 'Hindutva: Who is a Hindu?'. It tied Hindu identity more to land, race and culture than to religion, and is seen as the founding document of Hindu nationalism.
Bhakti movement

A medieval current of saint-poets such as Kabir, Raidas, Mirabai and Tukaram, who spoke of direct access to God. Many Bhakti poets questioned caste and ritual, though according to Ambedkar the movement could not break the caste system.
photo_note: Kabir at the loom, Mughal painting

h: Sijimali's Adivasis: holding on to their land amid arrests
dek: In the villages of Odisha's Rayagada and Kalahandi standing against bauxite mining, there are police camps, court cases and sal trees being cut, but the gram sabhas are demanding their rights.
body: Ranjana Padhi, a Bhubaneswar writer and feminist activist, writes in The Wire after returning from Odisha's Sijimali hills, where Adivasi (indigenous) villages spread across Rayagada and Kalahandi districts have stood for years against Vedanta's bauxite project. The project began with an agreement in February 2023, and in December 2025 it received only preliminary forest clearance.

According to the writer, a large number of sal trees have been cut on the hills. Narengi Dei Majhi of the Maa Maati Maali Suraksha Manch, who spent seven or eight months in jail last year, says at least thirty tractors carried the timber away, and no one knows whose order it was. Sal is a sacred tree for Adivasis.

In Talampadar village, police detained 21 Adivasis one night in March, 11 of them women. The women got bail after 44 days, and ten men got bail in June because the police could not file a chargesheet within 90 days. Just going to and from court costs three to four thousand rupees, and their wages have been lost.

In Kantamal, after a harsh police action six months ago, the police have come back and camped in the village community hall. Villagers allege that the signatures and thumbprints in the reports of the December 2023 gram sabha (village assembly) were forged. Now both Talampadar and Kantamal have called gram sabhas under the Forest Rights Act, formed forest rights committees and passed resolutions against the mining. The writer sees this as a violation of the protection given to Scheduled Areas under the PESA Act and Article 244(1).

She also asks who the Adivasis' real friends are. In the Odisha bandh of 8 October the opposition raised the issue of amendments to the mineral law, but according to the writer the demand to protect land, sacred sites and livelihoods is yet to be properly heard.
nazar: Sijimali's story recalls Niyamgiri, where the gram sabhas said no to mining. The Forest Rights Act is now twenty years old, yet it has not been implemented in these villages, while the police camps arrived first.

For people named in FIRs with words like '50 others', every court date is a punishment. If development comes without the consent of the gram sabha, it is a going back on the promise of the Constitution's Fifth Schedule.
sawal: Who will pay the price of the gram sabha's no?
ref: Forest Rights Act (2006)
A law that gives individual and community forest rights to Adivasis and forest-dependent communities. Under it, the consent of the gram sabha is considered necessary before forest land is used.
PESA Act (1996)
The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, which gives the gram sabha important rights over land and resources in Fifth Schedule areas.

h: From France to Albania: a season of revolt, and the far right's gain
dek: The French student movement that began with run-down schools has become a general revolt against the cost of living, and the writer fears Marine Le Pen may reap its political fruit.
body: In France in September, students of state high schools took to the streets against shrinking resources and broken buildings. By last week the movement had become a revolt of every section of society against the cost of living. In Dawn, columnist Mahir Ali writes that there was vandalism and arson on the fringes, but the big marches stayed peaceful and festive.

According to the writer, President Macron had nothing to offer beyond punishing the guilty and promising talks, and the announcement of 3,000 temporary teachers for students is not enough. Citing public debt of 119 percent of GDP, spending on education and health is held back, whereas by economists' reckoning a small rise in inheritance tax on the richest one percent of heirs alone would make a big investment in education possible.

The writer links this to unrest across Europe. In Spain, 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home of 70 years after she could not pay a 230 percent rent rise, and she died two weeks later. Spain votes on 29 November. In Portugal, Belgium, Italy and Albania too there are protests against costly housing and the arbitrariness of those in power.

The writer's biggest worry is that Marine Le Pen, who blames migrants for every problem, could profit from this upheaval. According to him, La France Insoumise is the only effective force of the Left there, and if Jean-Luc Mélenchon reaches the second round, Macron's centre would probably line up behind Le Pen.

The writer recalls 1968, when students and workers shook Charles de Gaulle's rule, and the student movement of 1968-69 in Pakistan that brought down Ayub Khan. But he regrets that even after the roof of a private school in Peshawar collapsed, killing 34 children and a teacher, no national accounting of education spending is being demanded in Pakistan.
nazar: This article shows that Europe's anger is not one country's story but the product of the same pressure of rents, fees and budget cuts that is felt from Karachi to Paris. When governments cite debt to avoid even fixing a school roof but put off talk of taxing the rich, the street is the only road left.
The danger is that the far right turns this anger against migrants. The movement's real demands, good schools and affordable homes, could be drowned in that noise.
sawal: Will the anger on the street go to the Left or to Le Pen?
ref: May 1968
A period of student revolt and a general strike by millions of workers in France, which shook the de Gaulle government and left a deep mark on European politics.
La France Insoumise
The French left-wing party led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, which calls for more social spending and taxing the rich.

h: Europe in crisis, Muslims in the firing line
dek: Amid the riots in France, a resolution on 'Islamist infiltration' passed in the European Parliament is, according to the writer, an attempt to paint anti-racism work itself as a conspiracy.
body: After protests in France turned violent, far-right leaders blamed young Muslims, migrants arriving in Ceuta in Spain were called an 'invasion', and Donald Trump described the unrest as an attempt at an Islamic takeover. Farid Hafez of Georgetown University's Bridge Initiative writes in Al Jazeera that the real worry is that blaming Muslims is no longer confined to the far right.

In these same days, the European Parliament passed a resolution on a strategy to tackle 'Islamist infiltration' and Muslim Brotherhood networks by 381 votes to 167. It was moved by the centre-right European People's Party, to which Commission President Ursula von der Leyen belongs, and was backed by far-right groups as well as the liberal Renew Europe.

According to the writer, the resolution treats a wide web of Muslim institutions, education, charity and youth groups as suspect, and says anti-discrimination structures can be used for the politics of religious identity. It also calls for stopping European funds to groups such as the Brussels-based European Network Against Racism. The writer recalls that the United Arab Emirates has for years funded campaigns that brand people as Brotherhood.

The resolution is not binding, but according to the writer its biggest effect is that efforts to protect Muslims from racism are now being called an Islamist conspiracy. In his view, the target of European Islamophobia is now Muslims who speak for themselves and defend civil liberties.

The phrase 'Islamo-leftism' in France is part of this, used to accuse Mélenchon of inciting rioters. The writer compares it to the old 'Judeo-Bolshevik' conspiracy story and says the answer is a strong defence of civil liberties for everyone.
nazar: When a movement born of budget cuts and rising prices is made to wear the glasses of religion, the real questions vanish. This method is not unfamiliar to readers in India, where too a conspiracy by some community is sought behind every social unrest.
The article's gravest warning is that centrist parties are now adopting the language of the far right. When fighting racism itself comes under suspicion, the wall of democracy weakens from within.
sawal: Since when did fighting racism become a conspiracy?
ref: European People's Party
The largest centre-right group in the European Parliament, which includes parties such as Germany's CDU.
Islamo-leftism
A phrase pushed in right-wing and government circles in France that accuses leftists of sympathy with Islamist extremism.

h: A peace prize, but no country: a Rohingya's appeal
dek: The Rohingya activist who won the Kofi Annan Youth Peace Prize says the world honours a few exceptions among refugees but does not break down the walls in the way of the rest.
body: On 15 October Rohingya human rights activist Maung Sawyeddollah received the first Kofi Annan Youth Peace Prize in Geneva. In The Daily Star he writes that he has a degree and has spoken before world leaders, yet Myanmar, where he was born, still does not recognise him as a citizen.

During the 2017 military campaign he fled with his family as a teenager. Reaching Bangladesh took about 15 days, and on the way his mother gave birth to a child. People there gave them food and shelter, for which he is grateful, but he says gratitude does not mean silence. The limits of the Cox's Bazar camps shrank his future, and without recognised documents he could not get into university.

In December 2019 he founded the Rohingya Students Network. After earning a degree through online study he reached New York University, but he refuses to see this only as an example of courage: other refugees being left behind is a lack of opportunity, not of ambition.

The writer believes the burden on Bangladesh should not fall on one country alone. He asks donors, universities and relief agencies to widen recognised education, accepted certificates and scholarships, through plans made together with refugees. His complaint is that refugees are invited to conferences to recount their pain, but their voice is little heard in decisions about return and education.

For a lasting solution he calls accountability for atrocities, restoration of citizenship and a safe, voluntary and dignified return to Myanmar essential. He dedicates the prize to every Rohingya student studying in a bamboo hut and wants his story to be not a comforting exception but a challenge to injustice.
nazar: More than ten lakh Rohingya have been in camps for nearly a decade, and the world's attention is now on other wars. A refugee saying he should be seen not as a witness but as the architect of his own future is a question for the whole humanitarian system.
It is also a mirror for all of South Asia, India included, where stateless people are often seen only as a security threat.
sawal: Who will give stateless young people the right to study?
ref: Rohingya
A Muslim minority community from Myanmar's Rakhine state, denied citizenship since the 1982 citizenship law.
Cox's Bazar
A coastal district of Bangladesh where more than ten lakh Rohingya live in one of the world's largest refugee settlements.

h: A map for peace in Ukraine: neutrality, a ceasefire line and limits on NATO
dek: Jeffrey Sachs and Sybil Fares propose a deal that treats the roots of the war, not its symptoms, guaranteed by all five permanent members of the Security Council.
body: As American envoys shuttle between Kyiv and Moscow, Columbia University economists Jeffrey Sachs and Sybil Fares have laid out a full peace framework in Common Dreams. They claim the war can end on terms that preserve the Ukrainian state, answer Russia's security concerns and build a lasting security order in Europe.

The proposal has four pillars. Ukraine should adopt permanent neutrality in law, like Austria in 1955, joining no alliance but keeping an army for its own defence. It should become a member of the European Union as a neutral country, and Russia should accept this. The front line on the day of signing should become the ceasefire line, but neither side should recognise the other's territorial claims. And NATO should withdraw its 2008 Bucharest promise and announce an end to eastward expansion.

The writers suggest making the Ukrainian-held part of Donetsk a demilitarised special zone, and in return Russia withdrawing from Dnipropetrovsk and the Kinburn Spit. The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant would stay with Russia under international monitoring and supply a fixed share of power to Ukraine at cost. Commercial shipping in the Black Sea would stay open.

There is also a proposal to ban ground-based intermediate-range missiles in Europe, restore the NATO-Russia Council and hand monitoring to the OSCE. All prisoners of war should be exchanged and separated children should return home. Sanctions should be lifted in 2027 and reconstruction on both sides funded by a European Investment Bank fund, with Russia also contributing as part of a shared effort.

The deal should be passed under Chapter VII of the Security Council and guaranteed by all five permanent members. The writers say Europe has so far been almost absent from shaping a peace plan, while this war has taken hundreds of thousands of lives and the danger of a clash between two nuclear powers remains.
nazar: It is easy to disagree with this proposal. For Ukraine, leaving Donetsk and giving up the Zaporizhzhia plant are bitter terms, and the question of Russia's accountability is blurred in it. Still, it breaks the inertia in which every side is only preparing for next winter's attacks.
From the Global South's point of view, what matters is that any road to peace should come not from bargaining among two or three capitals but through the United Nations and shared guarantees.
sawal: Can neutrality bring Ukraine peace?
ref: Austria's neutrality
In 1955, in return for the withdrawal of Soviet and Western troops, Austria adopted permanent military neutrality through a constitutional law.
OSCE
The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, a forum born of the 1975 Helsinki Accords that includes Russia, the US and European countries.

h: If violence stops nominations, courts will not stay silent: Supreme Court
dek: On a complaint by the YSRCP in Andhra Pradesh's local body polls, the court asked the State Election Commission to consider extending the nomination deadline and to hold back the final list of candidates.
body: The Supreme Court has said that courts usually do not interfere in the election process, but when the fairness of an election is threatened by force, intimidation or illegal means, the hands of constitutional courts are not tied. According to a LiveLaw report, a bench of Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana said this while granting interim relief on a petition by the YSR Congress Party, the main opposition party in Andhra Pradesh.

The party alleges that about two-thirds of its candidates in the urban local body elections could not even file nominations because of violence, blocked roads and a breakdown of law and order. The party had gone to the High Court even before the election process began, seeking security arrangements, but on 15 October the High Court rejected this. A plea to extend the last date for nominations was also turned down.

The bench accepted that conducting elections is the constitutional duty of the State Election Commission and that courts respect this, so that elections finish on time and do not get tangled in litigation midway. But according to the court, the right to file a nomination is part of a free and fair election, and a fair election is part of the basic structure of the Constitution. Under Article 243ZA the Commission has a duty to ensure every candidate can file a nomination without obstruction, and when violence makes this duty meaningless, courts cannot look away.

The court noted that the party had sent written and email complaints to the Commission even before the process began, and had also produced videos showing the obstruction. Treating this as a strong case at first sight, the court asked the Commission to consider the demand to extend the nomination period and, instead of issuing the final list of candidates on 21 October, to wait until 23 October. The court made clear that it is not running the election itself; the decision rests with the Commission.
nazar: This ruling comes at a time when questions about the fairness of the bodies that run elections have travelled from the street to the court. The court has repeated a simple point: the Election Commission's independence does not mean an end to its accountability.

If opposition candidates cannot even reach the point of filing their papers, polling day becomes a mere ritual. The bigger question is why the Commission itself does not wake up earlier to such complaints.
sawal: If candidates are stopped from filing papers, how free is the election?
ref: Article 243ZA
The provision of the Constitution that gives the State Election Commission charge of preparing voter lists and overseeing elections to municipal bodies.
Basic structure doctrine
The principle, from the 1973 Kesavananda Bharati judgment, that some basic features of the Constitution cannot be changed by Parliament even through amendment.

h: Power and water cut, gates shut, yet prayers go on at the Race Course mosque
dek: A hundred-year-old mosque near the Prime Minister's residence has been called unauthorised on government land, and its imam has been told to vacate within six days.
body: On Tuesday, about ten people offered the zuhr (midday) prayer at the nearly hundred-year-old Race Course mosque near the Prime Minister's official residence in New Delhi, even though entry is restricted. According to a Maktoob Media report, security personnel first stopped them, saying there were orders from above, but the worshippers still got inside.

The mosque's electricity and water were cut on 7 October and its gates were locked. The Land and Development Office, or L&DO, has told imam Mohammad Haroon to vacate the place within six days. A notice put up there says the land belongs to the Government of India and warns of legal action over unauthorised occupation. The CPWD has been given the job of carrying it out.

Government papers, though, say something else. A Delhi Administration gazette notification of 8 September 1977 records this mosque behind Safdarjung's Tomb, along with the graveyard next to it, as a property of two bighas, and the NDMC counts it among heritage buildings. According to the imam, a 2021 survey also did not treat it as unauthorised. He says he had been knocking on the doors of the Delhi Waqf Board for six months, but got no real help. His family lives on the premises and now depends on a generator.

On Monday the Waqf Board wrote to the L&DO, asking for the mosque to be protected and its power and water restored. The letter says the mosque has had a legal electricity connection since 1976, and that the supply was cut without notice while nearby slums were being cleared. A delegation of the Jamiat Ulama-i-Hind met Minority Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju, who assured them of every possible effort. Asaduddin Owaisi pointed out that the board has not even been constituted since 2023, and Congress MP Syed Naseer Hussain called it bulldozer politics.
nazar: When a building that the government's own gazette and the municipal council treat as heritage is suddenly called unauthorised, it shows that papers matter only as long as those in power want them to. Cutting power and water without notice is a way of slowly draining the life out of a place of worship.

The Waqf Board, which is supposed to protect such properties, has not even been constituted for three years. This mix of official harshness and institutional neglect is causing deep unease among Delhi's Muslims.
sawal: Who will decide who is unauthorised on whose land?
ref: Land and Development Office (L&DO)
An office under the Union Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs that manages land leased out by the central government in Delhi.
Waqf Board
A state-level statutory body that looks after and protects mosques, graveyards and Muslim properties given in charity.

h: Second time in three weeks: Satish Acharya's Instagram blocked in India
dek: The cartoonist's recent cartoons were about how Delhi Police handled protests against the Chief Election Commissioner, and nobody has given a reason for blocking the account.
body: Political cartoonist Satish Acharya's Instagram account was blocked in India again on Tuesday, the second time this has happened in three weeks. According to a Scroll report, opening the account shows a Meta message saying access has been temporarily restricted because of legal requirements under the IT Rules. It is not clear what led to the order this time.

Acharya posted a screenshot of the blocked account on X and took a dig at the government, saying it was elected to bring 'achhe din' (good days) but is wasting its term shutting down Instagram accounts. He asked who exactly is so scared of cartoons. On 20 October he had written that the protest frame on his profile would stay until those in power stop fearing political cartoons.

The account was first blocked on 28 September on a legal request from the government and was restored on 5 October. Under the 2021 IT Rules, a platform has to take down allegedly unlawful content within three hours of getting a direction from the government or a court. At around the same time, another cartoonist, Manjul, also had his work on the Election Commission blocked in India. Acharya's recent cartoons were on Delhi Police's conduct at protests against Gyanesh Kumar, and on BJP leader Dushyant Kumar Gautam being made Governor of Sikkim, while the CBI is investigating him in a murder case.

The report places this in a larger pattern. Between March and July, the government sent nearly two lakh orders to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, or about 1,275 a day, and each order can cover hundreds of posts or accounts. Citing records obtained under the Right to Information, it says 2,312 blocking orders were sent to 19 platforms through the Sahyog portal between October 2024 and October 2025.
nazar: Cartoons are democracy's oldest habit of laughing at power. When a cartoonist's entire wall is plunged into darkness without a reason and without a hearing, it looks less like action against one post and more like an attempt to frighten a whole form of criticism.

Platforms are plugged straight into a government portal and carry out orders, and the user does not even learn whose complaint it is. Someone being silenced should at least have the right to know why.
sawal: How much of a threat is one cartoon to a government?
ref: Sahyog portal
An online portal of the Union Home Ministry through which government agencies send content takedown notices directly to platforms.
IT Rules 2021
Rules for social media and digital media that require platforms to follow government directions and keep a grievance system.

h: Rubio waves off UN experts, then heads to Ambani's refinery
dek: The US Secretary of State brushed aside the question of the crackdown on protesters in India as an internal matter, and spent the day with Adani, Tata and Reliance.
body: Speaking to journalists at the Taj Mahal Palace hotel in Mumbai on Wednesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed as self-contradictory the United Nations experts who had raised concern over the crackdown on protests in India and the mistreatment of young people and women. According to The Wire's report, Rubio said he would not comment on India's internal politics, because India holds elections and is a democracy.

Rubio argued that protests can be a sign of healthy political debate in any country. He compared India with Cuba, where, he said, opposition figures cannot escape jail, repression or exile, and set peaceful protests apart from the riots in Europe that involved vandalism and arson. The report recalls that the Trump administration has pulled out of several UN bodies, including the UN Human Rights Council, and that six US lawmakers had asked Rubio to raise the excessive use of force against protesters during this visit.

On the second day of his visit, Rubio began with closed-door meetings with Gautam Adani and Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran. This was Adani's first meeting with a senior Trump administration minister since the criminal case against him in the US was dropped in August.

Rubio then went to Reliance's refinery in Jamnagar, Gujarat, the world's largest single-site refinery, which processes about 14 lakh barrels of crude oil a day. Its ability to refine heavy crude matters to the US, which is looking for markets for Venezuela's rising oil output. The programme included a visit to Vantara and dinner with Mukesh Ambani, but the company did not announce any concrete investment.
nazar: It may be a relief for the Indian government that the world's biggest power has looked away from the question of repression. But dismissing human rights concerns and sitting down to oil business with billionaires on the same day shows what price democracy fetches on Washington's scales.
India's protesters do not need a certificate from any foreign government, but it is worth remembering that business friendships are often kept up at the cost of civil liberties.
sawal: Did oil deals outweigh the voice of human rights?
ref: Vantara
Reliance's large animal rescue and rehabilitation centre in Jamnagar, set up at the initiative of Anant Ambani.
UN Human Rights Council
The United Nations body that monitors human rights in member countries and appoints independent experts.

h: London SIR protest: 'Pakistani flag' pictures turn out to be made with AI
dek: A BOOM fact-check found that both pictures linked to the protest led by Dhruv Rathee were fake and the video was old.
body: After an anti-SIR protest in London led by YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, claims spread on social media that Pakistani and Bangladeshi nationals had joined it carrying their flags. Fact-check website BOOM looked into these claims and found that two pictures passed around as proof had been made or altered with AI, and that a video was two months old and had nothing to do with this protest.

According to BOOM, on 18 October the official handle of the BJP's Delhi unit put out a post alleging that Rahul Gandhi and Arvind Kejriwal had gathered people in London to defame India. Some content creators shared a picture of a man named Saddam Hussain Makrani holding a Pakistani flag and called him Pakistani. Another user posted a video of people waving Pakistani flags alongside the tricolour to the song 'Jai Ho' and said the protest was full of Pakistanis.

The check found Makrani's real picture on his Instagram, in which he is holding a phone, not a flag. Makrani himself released a video saying he is an Indian citizen, has lived in Britain for six years, and that a five-year-old picture of his had been tampered with. When BOOM ran the altered picture through an AI detection tool, it found a digital watermark, which made it clear that it had been changed with an AI tool. The picture of young men draped in Bangladeshi flags was found to be entirely AI-generated.

The 'Jai Ho' video was posted on the Instagram of Pakistani-origin singer Aamir Hashmi in August 2026. According to Hashmi's post, it was an event at Piccadilly Circus in London on 15 August, marking the independence days of both India and Pakistan. BOOM has rated all the claims false.
nazar: Calling people who question the voter rolls 'Pakistani' is now a tried and tested trick, and AI has made it cheap and fast. When the official unit of a ruling party is counted among those spreading such material, it is hard to call it a mere misunderstanding.

The hardest blow fell on an ordinary man whose old picture was picked up and who was turned into an enemy overnight. In such cases, the duty to apologise and correct lies as much with those who posted it as with the platform.
sawal: Who will be held accountable for lies made with AI?
ref: SIR (Special Intensive Revision)
The Election Commission's house-to-house check of the voter rolls. The opposition and citizen groups allege it is being used to cut names on a large scale.

h: Fake video on Neha Singh Rathore: three ABP staff face the axe
dek: According to Newslaundry Hindi, the channel apologised after running a false story, and sources say three people lost their jobs.
body: ABP News has acted against three of its employees over a false and insulting video it ran about folk singer and satirist Neha Singh Rathore. Citing sources, a Newslaundry Hindi report says the head of video production, the video shift in-charge and the YouTube Shorts in-charge have been removed. The channel has made no official announcement about this. In public it has only apologised.

The case concerns a video run on ABP's digital platform that claimed a sex racket was operating in the hostel where Neha used to live and that police had raided it. According to the report, the claim was first made by a social media handle and the channel picked it up as it was, without any attempt to get Neha's side. On 17 October the channel apologised on X for the wrong broadcast. The National Commission for Women took note of the matter on its own and has asked the channel for an action-taken report within fifteen days.

Neha says the clip used in the video is of a 2024 police raid on a spa centre, not a hostel, and that the picture of her used was from an interview she gave ABP three years ago. She questioned the channel's executive vice president Rajneesh Ahuja on the phone and made a video of that conversation public. She says an apology is not enough, because this was no small slip, her name was attached to it, and she will file a defamation case.

The report also points to pressure inside the newsroom. According to sources, staff are asked for a count of views every hour, there is a separate five-person team for Shorts, and producers are also put to editing short videos. Newslaundry called Ahuja and sent questions by email, but had no reply by the time the report was published.
nazar: One apology and three sackings after throwing mud on a woman's reputation is an incomplete reckoning. The real question is about a system that counts views every hour but leaves no time to check facts.
Neha Singh Rathore is known for her sharp songs against those in power. The question is also why such 'slips' by mainstream channels so often land on voices that question power.
sawal: In the race for views, who pays the price of the truth?
ref: National Commission for Women
A statutory body set up in 1992 that hears complaints about women's rights. It can take up a matter on its own and seek a response.

h: Manipur SIR: two-thirds of 1.59 lakh deleted names are from the hills
dek: According to an early report by the Saber Institute, two and a half times more names were removed at hill booths than in the valley, and most of those removed are women.
body: In Manipur, 1,58,677 names have been removed in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter rolls, and about two-thirds of them are from hill assembly constituencies. SabrangIndia has published these details, citing an early report by the Saber Institute. The report, by Sabir Ahmed, Souptik Halder and Ashin Chakraborty, is based on the lists of absent, shifted and dead voters released by the Chief Electoral Officer, and covers 3,014 booths across all 60 seats in the state.

According to the report, 1,05,294 names were cut in the 20 hill seats, which is 66.4 per cent of the total. There, an average of 79 names were removed per booth, while in the 39 valley seats the average is around 31. Churachandpur district alone lost 38,264 names, more than Imphal East and Imphal West put together. Saikot seat tops the list, with 14,152 names removed across 84 booths. Of the 20 hill seats, 19 are reserved for Scheduled Tribes.

The reasons differ too. In the valley, death is recorded as the biggest reason, while in the hills half the names were removed on the grounds of having permanently moved elsewhere, and about a quarter for being absent. The report accepts that the lists do not show who was displaced by the violence that began in May 2023 and who left by choice. About 56 per cent of those removed are women, and in every seat they outnumber men.

The authors say clearly that these figures do not prove names were wrongly cut or that any community was deliberately left out. Rather, they show where checking should begin. Their recommendations are: booth-by-booth verification starting with the booths that lost the most names, a simple process for objections and appeals, free legal aid, human oversight of automated tools, and scrutiny in Parliament. The report does not include any response from the Election Commission or the state government.
nazar: In a state where thousands of families have been in relief camps for years, cutting names by writing 'moved elsewhere' can amount to making people pay for their displacement with their right to vote. If booth-level checks confirm this pattern, it will directly hurt the representation of the Adivasi (indigenous) population in the hill areas.
The Election Commission should make booth-wise data and the basis for every deleted name public, so that evidence, not suspicion, does the talking.
sawal: Where does a displaced voter go to save their name?
ref: ASD list
The list of Absent, Shifted and Dead voters that election officials publish before removing names.
Manipur violence, May 2023
Violence that broke out between the Meitei and Kuki-Zo communities, in which more than 250 people were killed and more than sixty thousand were displaced.

h: Yak herders of Bhutan, India and Nepal to form a shared network
dek: Amid shrinking pastures, changing weather and falling yak numbers, Himalayan herders are coming together on a regional platform for the first time.
body: Yak herders from Bhutan, India and Nepal are together forming the Himalayan Yak Herders Network. According to a Down To Earth report, it is being described as the first regional network of yak-herding communities in the Himalaya, and it will be launched on 23 October at Bhutan's ninth Royal Highland Festival. According to the intergovernmental body ICIMOD, its aim is cross-border cooperation, sharing knowledge, building capacity and speaking up together.

The herders face a long list of problems: shrinking pastures, climate change, a falling yak population, attacks by wild animals, degrading grasslands, declining diversity of yak breeds, poor access to markets and basic services, and young people leaving the high areas. ICIMOD studies show that yak numbers have fallen sharply in all three countries over the past few decades, partly because of changes in land use and the poor state of pastures.

India's figures point the same way. The 20th Livestock Census, published in 2019, recorded about 58 thousand yaks in the country. In 2026 the Yak Federation of India said its 526 member families together rear about 32 thousand yaks. The two figures cannot be compared directly, though, as the federation counts only its own members.

Nearly a decade of joint work lies behind this network. The idea came up in 2016, when herders, researchers and government representatives from the three countries met under ICIMOD's Kangchenjunga Landscape Initiative. It will include the Yak Federation of India, the Bhutan Yak Federation and Nepal's Yak and Chauri Farmers Federation. It will be run by the yak herders themselves, and its secretariat will be in Bhutan. According to the organisers, more than 60 per cent of the Hindu Kush Himalaya is grassland, and 2.5 to 3 crore indigenous people of many different cultures depend on it.
nazar: Borders exist on maps; pastures and weather do not recognise them. At a time when South Asia's governments are caught up in mutual distrust, herders building their own shared platform offers hope that mountain people will speak for themselves.
In India, the voices of yak herders in Ladakh, Sikkim and Arunachal rarely reach the policy table. This network could give them a voice, provided governments are ready to listen.
sawal: Will herders' voices reach the policies made for the Himalaya?
ref: ICIMOD
An intergovernmental body based in Kathmandu with eight Hindu Kush Himalaya countries as members. It works on the mountain environment and people's livelihoods.
Chauri
An animal born from crossing a yak and a cow, reared in the high areas of Nepal for milk and for carrying loads.

h: As the Ganga treaty nears its end, Bihar asks for its share of water
dek: The India-Bangladesh Ganga water treaty expires this year, and Bihar says it supplies water for Farakka but its own needs are not counted anywhere.
body: The Ganga water-sharing treaty signed between India and Bangladesh in December 1996 runs out this year. The treaty sets how the river's flow at the Farakka Barrage is shared in the dry months from January to June. If the flow is below 70,000 cusecs, the water is split half and half.

According to this Mongabay India report, Bihar's leaders say the treaty paid no attention to the state's needs. JD(U) MP Sanjay Jha told the Rajya Sabha on 6 August that renewing the treaty without solving Bihar's long-term water security would be harmful. The state claims it has only 16 per cent of the Ganga's catchment area, yet half the dry-season water reaching Farakka comes from its tributaries.

For drinking and industry in the dry days, the JD(U) wants 2,000 cusecs of water, while an internal committee is said to have recommended 900 cusecs. Sunil Kumar Chaudhary, a former professor from Bhagalpur, wants a study of needs up to 2050 and a fixed share for Bihar, because both population and demand are growing.

But not everyone agrees with this demand. Himanshu Thakkar of SANDRP says there is no evidence that the treaty puts pressure on Bihar's flows. According to Rajiv Sinha of IIT Kanpur, the real problem is silt, which has kept building up upstream since Farakka was built. His team's study estimates that about 15.6 crore tonnes of silt may be getting trapped every year, which has made the river shallower around Bhagalpur.

According to the report, ending the treaty is not practical, because the Ganga is a river shared by two countries. Chaudhary wants joint management at the level of the whole basin, while Sinha demands that Bihar be treated as a stakeholder and that a condition on silt management be added to the new treaty.
nazar: The Farakka debate often ends up as diplomacy between Delhi and Dhaka, while the real price is paid by farmers and fishers along the Ganga and by villages drowning in floods. A river made shallow by silt makes floods worse and leaves less water in the dry season.
The new treaty should not stop at dividing cusecs. Giving riverside settlements, panchayats (village councils) and states a place at the table would be the fair way forward.
sawal: When a river is divided, where are the people who live on its banks?
ref: Ganga Water Treaty 1996
A 30-year agreement between India and Bangladesh that sets how the Ganga's water at Farakka is shared in the dry season.
Farakka Barrage
A barrage on the Ganga in West Bengal built between 1961 and 1975 to divert water into the Hooghly and keep Kolkata port working.

h: A murder in Malaysia: a twenty-year wait for justice for Altantuya
dek: This investigative film from Al Jazeera's 101 East asks whether power and politics still protect the people behind the 2006 killing of a Mongolian translator.
body: On 17 October, Al Jazeera's investigative series 101 East released 'Murder in Malaysia: Justice for Altantuya Shaariibuu'. The roughly 48-minute film returns to Malaysia's most talked-about and most tangled murder case, which took place twenty years ago. The film's basic question is whether power and politics are still protecting the people behind this killing.

Altantuya Shaariibuu was a 28-year-old translator from Mongolia. In October 2006 she was taken from outside the house of Abdul Razak Baginda in Kuala Lumpur, driven to a forest outside the city and shot, and then her body was blown up with C4, an explosive used by the military. Baginda was then an adviser to and close associate of Deputy Prime Minister Najib Razak, and had been in a relationship with Altantuya.

Two members of a special unit of the Malaysian police, Sirul Azhar Umar and Azilah Hadri, were convicted of the murder in 2009 and sentenced to death. Both were posted in Najib's security detail. But the courts could never establish why the killing was carried out. This missing motive is the crack through which suspicion of a political conspiracy has kept seeping out.

At the root of this suspicion is a multi-billion-dollar submarine deal with France, which has long faced allegations of corruption. Najib approved the deal in 2002 as defence minister, and Baginda was its middleman. According to Al Jazeera's earlier reporting, Altantuya had travelled to Paris with Baginda and was allegedly asking for money in return for her help with the deal.

According to the film's introduction, the 101 East team travels to Mongolia, Malaysia, France and Australia to connect the threads of this story. The investigation rests on three things: alleged interference in the criminal trial, Altantuya's suspected link to the submarine deal, and the claim by the convicted policemen that they acted on the orders of former Prime Minister Najib Razak. Najib, who is himself serving a sentence in a separate corruption case, denies any link to the killing.

Meanwhile, Altantuya's family has been seeking answers for twenty years. In 2022 a Malaysian civil court ordered the government, Baginda and the two policemen to pay the family damages. The film puts this long wait at its centre: the murder of a foreign woman whose killers were caught, but the name of whoever gave the order is still in the dark.
nazar: This case shows that when the threads of a crime seem to lead to the high corridors of power, justice often stops halfway: the hands that did it are punished, but the questions never reach the order.

A woman from a poor country, commissions on defence deals and secret units: this picture is not Malaysia's alone. In South Asia too, questions about arms deals and the nexus of power have stayed buried for years.
sawal: Is any justice complete without reaching the one who gave the order?
ref: 101 East
Al Jazeera English's investigative documentary series, focused on news and society in the Asia-Pacific region.
C4
A powerful military explosive. Altantuya's body was blown up with it, which deepened questions about the role of the army and the police.

h: Lucknow turning into malls and cafes: a city seen through Allahabad eyes
dek: Abhishek Kumar Singh's essay on Hindwi's Bela looks at Lucknow through the eyes of Allahabad, as the old city slowly turns into malls and cafes.
body: Abhishek Kumar Singh's essay, published on Hindwi's blog Bela on 21 October, is half memoir and half survey of a city. The writer says he is staying in Lucknow's Gomti Nagar for a government training programme, and had come here before for his studies too. In his view, a stay of a few days can only just touch a city.

The first thing he notices is what looks like an effort to make Lucknow like Chandigarh: cafes, gyms, pubs and shops copying Mumbai and Delhi. Compared with Allahabad, he finds the political swagger here a little less, the pollution lower and the traffic better. Through an informal mehfil (gathering) with a poet from the Urdu Academy, he tells us that some poets of the old city make watches for a living and recite their verses only in their own neighbourhood.

A large part of the essay is about markets and food. Chikankari is better and cheaper in Chowk than in expensive showrooms, but there is also a risk of fakes. In malls, ittar (traditional perfume) is now sold next to deodorant. He finds the Rumi Darwaza beautiful, but there are no guides there to explain the heritage, only people getting their photos taken.

The most interesting part is about the city's changing cultural life. According to the writer, institutions like the Hindi Sansthan and the Urdu Academy have gone sluggish, while a new buzz of open mics and theatre has grown up around cafes. Lucknow University's old student politics is almost over. The market is bridging the gap between old and new Lucknow: the old city reaches the malls as decorative imitation, and cafes keep moving into the old city.
At the end he recalls an acquaintance from Allahabad saying that Lucknow is a city stuck somewhere between the depth of Lahore and the glitter of Delhi, and he thinks this is partly true.
nazar: This essay is not a marsiya (elegy) for a historic Lucknow, but an honest account of a mid-sized city whose story is becoming the story of every town and city. The drying up of cultural institutions and the rise of cafes show that public culture is now shrinking into places of buying and selling.

If the city of Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb (the shared Hindu-Muslim culture of north India) turns into mall decoration, the question is what room will be left for those poets who make watches and write verse.
sawal: Are our cities becoming copies of themselves?
ref: Rumi Darwaza
Lucknow's famous gateway, built in the late eighteenth century during the time of Asaf-ud-Daula, the Nawab of Awadh.
Chikankari
Lucknow's tradition of fine embroidery in white thread, which has been the city's identity for centuries.

h: One Dussehra, two memories: Durga's victory and the mourning for Hudur Durga
dek: Baby Shaw's essay shows that in the very days Bengal celebrates the goddess's victory, the Santhal and other Adivasi communities remember the defeat of their ancestor.
body: This instalment of Baby Shaw's series 'C/O Bengal' on Hindwi's Bela was published on 20 October. It opens with the immersion at the end of Durga Puja: the sound of the dhak (drum), flying sindoor (vermilion), women in red-bordered white saris bidding farewell, and a naughty boy stuffing a rasgulla into the mouth of the asura (demon) idol. The crowd laughs, but one man does not. The writer describes him as being like a character from Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay's novel 'Aranyak' (Of the Forest).

The essay rests on this contradiction. For Bengal, Vijayadashami is the goddess's victory, where Durga is both Mahishasuramardini, the slayer of the buffalo demon, and Uma, the daughter come home. The writer also reminds us that the story of Ram's akal-bodhan, his worship of Durga before the war with Ravan, is not found in Valmiki's Ramayan, and gained a special place in the Bangla Ramayan of the fifteenth-century poet Krittibas Ojha.

On the other side, Santhal and other Adivasi communities in Jangalmahal and many parts of Jharkhand remember Mahishasur as Hudur Durga, an ancestral king and warrior. According to the writer, in folklore he was killed by deceit: a woman was sent, and when she came before him with weapons, Hudur Durga laid down his arms because of a rule against fighting a woman. In this story it is the killing of an unarmed hero, not a fair fight.

From this memory came the Dansai dance, in which men wear saris, put on peacock feathers and play the bhuang, made from a dried gourd, as they search for their lost king. According to the writer, this festival is observed at about 300 places in West Bengal, and in some villages no lamp is lit during the days of the puja.
The essay concludes that the same festival holds different meanings for different communities, and that respect for every community's memory is the true wealth of Indian culture.
nazar: This essay comes at a time when the push to bind festivals to a single story and a single feeling has grown. The memory of Hudur Durga shows that Adivasi society has its own memories, and dismissing them as a 'distortion' is like erasing their identity.
The writer does not call either side false. She keeps both stories side by side, and that is the simplest lesson in plurality.
sawal: When we celebrate one victory, whose defeat do we forget?
ref: Dansai
A traditional dance and festival of the Santhal community, held around Durga Puja and linked to the search for a lost ancestor.
Aranyak
Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay's 1939 Bangla novel about the forests of Bihar and the Adivasi life there.

h: A voter in a lungi and a black fish: Selim Mallik's Bangla poems in Hindi
dek: Sammukh carries six poems by Bengal poet Selim Mallik, translated by Suparna Mandal, that move between love, election-time fear, death and language.
by: Selim Mallik, translated by Suparna Mandal
body: On 16 October, Sammukh published six poems by Bangla poet Selim Mallik in Hindi translation. According to the introduction, Mallik was born in 1977 in a village in Purba Medinipur, works in publishing and editing, brings out a magazine called 'Astrik', and has published five collections of poetry. He has received several honours, including the Krittibas Award. Translator Suparna Mandal is doing research in comparative literature at Visva-Bharati and teaches English at a government degree college in Bihar.

The first poem touches the episode at the start of the Ramayan where a couple's union breaks into weeping, and reads it as this country's first great story. By the end it becomes a restlessness at not being able to understand this country and its upper classes, and a memory of a home left behind.

The second poem is the most political in the set. A couple in love wake up on the morning of the vote, uniformed jawans (soldiers) arrive, and then calm returns to the area. But the poem lingers on the image of an old Muslim man who was not allowed into the polling booth because he was wearing a lungi. Here even the calm carries a layer of fear.

The other poems turn inward. In one, after the poet's death, a black fish circles among his things, while a broken loom and a dried-up pond are left behind. One poem asks, amid noise and garbage, whether we can ever talk in the language of flowers again. The poem 'Language' says that living memories and the dead both live inside language, and the last poem is about a faint scent left in an empty house. See the Sammukh link to read the poems in full.
nazar: The lungi poem says a big truth in a small picture: on paper everyone has the right to vote, but it can be blocked by what you wear and who you are. When questions of trust in the electoral process are out on the streets, this poem feels even sharper.
Contemporary Bangla poetry rarely reaches Hindi. Translators like Suparna Mandal are building this bridge between two neighbouring languages.
sawal: Whose clothes are checked before they can vote?
ref: Krittibas Award
A well-known honour for Bangla poetry, named after the fifteenth-century poet Krittibas Ojha.
Visva-Bharati
The university founded by Rabindranath Tagore, in Santiniketan, West Bengal.

h: Four poets, four books and one question in Lucknow
dek: Four new poetry collections came out at a Jan Sanskriti Manch evening, and the debate settled on whether today's poetry is catching the voice of its time.
body: Samkaleen Janmat has published a report on a literary evening in Lucknow. Under its series 'Chaar Kavi, Chaar Kitaabein' (Four Poets, Four Books), the Lucknow unit of Jan Sanskriti Manch launched four poetry collections on 11 October in the hall of the Kaifi Azmi Academy. The books were Shailesh Pandit's 'Akele Aadmi Ki Lau' (The Flame of a Lonely Man), Umesh Pankaj's 'Mitti Hain Hum' (We Are Earth), Vimal Kishore's 'Phir Khil Uthenge' (We Will Bloom Again) and Kaushal Kishore's 'Duniya Ki Sabse Sundar Kavita' (The Most Beautiful Poem in the World). All four poets read selected poems.

The evening was chaired by Faizabad poet, fiction writer and critic Swapnil Srivastava. In his view, all four are poets who give shape to the contradictions of their time. Their poetry holds today's sorrow, joy and resistance, and speaks of the people still left on the margins in the race for development. The themes are similar, but each poet's language is different.

In the second session each book was discussed separately. Young critic Ashish Singh traced in Umesh Pankaj's poems a journey from the personal to the political and a recognition of the repressive face of power. He also raised a big question, citing Trilochan: the job of poetry is not to record events or give information, but to catch the voice of its time, and how far is today's poetry managing that. Usha Rai counted three streams in Vimal Kishore's collection: women's lives and the violence against them; poems against nationalism, fascism, consumerism and lynching; and poems on nature and the Covid years.

Prof. Suraj Bahadur Thapa described Kaushal Kishore's book as centred on many sides of women's lives, with poems on mothers, on love and on activists like Seema Azad. Prof. Nalin Ranjan Singh saw in Shailesh Pandit's poems the ordinary person's clash with the present system, including poems on electoral 'infiltrators', on Manipur and on Gaza, and a geography stretching from the village to the Northeast. The evening was hosted by Farzana Mahdi.
nazar: Far from the glitter of big publishers and literature festivals, evenings like this are the real ground of Hindi poetry, where a book's politics is discussed as openly as the book. That Gaza, Manipur, lynching and the 'infiltrator' debate appear across the four collections shows that poetry is not looking away from its time.
Ashish Singh's question is the most valuable thing about this evening. Breaking the news into lines is not poetry, and committed poetry has to apply this test to itself.
sawal: Is today's poetry able to go beyond the news?
ref: Jan Sanskriti Manch
An organisation of left-wing writers, artists and cultural workers formed in 1985, which holds literary and cultural events in many cities.
Trilochan
A progressive Hindi poet (1917-2007), known for his sonnets and for simple poetry rooted in folk life.

h: The fair of protest and the reel makers: a satire by Rachit
dek: Rachit's new satire in Hindwi's 'Bela' says this country is made of fairs, and that the reel makers at today's sit-ins are part of the same fair.
body: This time, Rachit's column 'Reel Rasacharya' (Master of Reel Flavours) on Hindwi's blog 'Bela' is about the relationship between protests on the streets and the people who make reels. It begins with a big claim: India is a fair in itself. Whether it was the Portuguese, Dutch, French and English traders who came looking for spices, or the poets, jugglers and families who travelled with armies, everything here eventually takes the shape of a fair.

According to the writer, the freedom struggle was the same fair, where people sang and spun the charkha (spinning wheel) amid police guns. He links Himanshu Kumar spinning the charkha at today's Jantar Mantar to that same tradition. His argument is that the presence of reel makers at today's sit-ins does not weaken the spirit of a movement, because a movement is made not of new ideas but of many voices repeating one thing.

Then come the characters of this fair. An old man famous for reels advertising male virility medicines, who now backs the movement at the sit-in with his deep voice. Rakhi Sawant, whom the writer calls an 'art form', and whose arrival at the Mumbai protest drew a large section of people to the movement. And a short young man named Nikhil Verma who, according to the piece, went viral for his peculiar run during a lathi charge and became the crowd's favourite.

In the end the writer turns the edge of the satire on himself. He admits that some people may go to sit-ins just for reels, but the bigger hypocrisy is that of the commentator who forms opinions sitting at home. He compares himself to Sanjay of the Mahabharat, who never went to the battlefield and simply narrated what he saw. See the Hindwi link to read the full column.
nazar: It is easy to dismiss reels as a frivolous part of a movement, but Rachit reminds us that in this country resistance has always moved along with songs, spectacle and crowds. The young man who goes viral running from a lathi is also standing on the same street.
The most honest part is the last one: the person who sits in front of a screen passing judgement on a movement is really the one furthest from it.
sawal: Is making reels at a sit-in participation or spectacle?
ref: Himanshu Kumar
A Gandhian social activist who worked for years among Adivasis in Dantewada, Chhattisgarh, and spoke up for their rights.
Sanjay
Dhritarashtra's charioteer in the Mahabharat, who was given divine sight and narrated the Kurukshetra war, as he saw it, to the king sitting in the palace.
